Need to search first.I couldn't open any full pages. A tool limit cut off direct page reads early, so these notes come only from the page text the search tool returned. That text was often partial, so many verses have thin coverage. Every point below comes from the page at its URL.

I found almost nothing that splits along denominational lines. I found no Methodist, Lutheran or Pentecostal source on this chapter, no Orthodox source, no NET Bible notes, and no prosperity or word-of-faith teaching on it. The real disagreements are between individual commentators, and I've marked them **[Debate]**. Where a page labels a writer's tradition, I give the label. Otherwise I don't.

**Main sources**
- Enduring Word (David Guzik): https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-10/ and his study guide at https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-kings/1-kings-10.cfm
- Pulpit Commentary: https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
- Gill (StudyLight calls him "Calvinist… Baptist"): https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/10.htm and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-10.html
- Ellicott: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-10.html
- Matthew Henry: https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-10.html and https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_010.cfm
- Constable: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-10.html
- Adam Clarke: https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-10.html
- Precept Austin: https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-10-commentary

---

**Whole chapter: how should Solomon's glory be read? [Debate]**
- **Positive.** Wealth and godliness don't have to be opposites, and this visit marks Israel's high point. The Church should make wealth serve religion. (Biblical Illustrator) https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-kings-10.html
- **Positive.** Henry says trade is no disgrace, and Solomon spread his wealth to his people instead of hoarding it. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_010.cfm
- **Warning.** The Pulpit Commentary sees signs of worldliness, maybe the turning point in his drift from God. It notes his life goes steadily downhill from here. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
- **Warning.** Expositor's Bible says Solomon encouraged outward worship, not spiritual life. It adds that Jesus valued the lilies of the field above this splendour. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/1_kings/10.htm
- **Warning.** Kelly asks whether this was really the king after God's heart, since God had warned kings against piling up wealth. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/10-10.html
- **Anglican view.** The Church Pulpit Commentary (StudyLight describes it as essays by Anglican writers) contrasts the ties with Tyre and Egypt, which brought no one to God, with the visit from Sheba. It calls the Sheba visit the true model of what Israel was meant to do for the nations. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/1-kings-10.html

---

**v. 1**
- **Where Sheba was.** Most sources place it in southern Arabia (Yemen):
  - The Pulpit Commentary sees no good reason to doubt this. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
  - Gill puts it in southern Arabia. He notes that Ethiopians call her Maqueda and an Arabic geographer calls her Belequis. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/10.htm
  - Henry says Ethiopian Christians claim her as theirs, but Arabia is more likely. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-10.html
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia places Saba in southern Arabia, about 200 miles northwest of Aden. https://www.newadvent.org/cathen/13285c.htm
- **"Fame… concerning the name of the LORD."** Barnes suggests it means Solomon's religious fame, his wisdom about God. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/10-1.html
- **How she heard.** One older comment on Bible Hub says she probably heard through Solomon's ships passing her coast. It speculates she was descended from Abraham through Keturah and so knew something of the true God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/10-1.htm
- **"Hard questions." [Debate]**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says they need not be only riddles and may well have included religious questions. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
  - Another commentator on the same Bible Hub page says Matthew 12:42 doesn't prove they were religious. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/10-1.htm
- **Pictures of Christ.**
  - Gill sees her as a picture of the Gentiles seeking Christ. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-10.html
  - Spurgeon preached on Jesus' "greater than Solomon" saying (Matthew 12:42). He argued that if she travelled so far for Solomon, people today have even less excuse not to come to Christ. https://www.spurgeon.org/resource-library/sermons/the-queen-of-sheba-a-sign/
- **Why she came.** Constable thinks her main aim was a treaty, and she wanted to check Solomon first. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-10.html
- **Modern scholarship.**
  - Bible Odyssey says the debate over where Sheba was is unresolved. Ancient lists of Sabaean rulers name only kings, so it calls a queen of Sheba "historically unlikely." https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/queen-of-sheba/
  - It also says the story's purpose is to show Solomon's wisdom was famous even at the edge of the known world. https://www.bibleodyssey.org/articles/queen-of-sheba/

**v. 2**
- **"Very large caravan."** The Hebrew can mean a "force." Thenius took it as an armed escort, which the Pulpit Commentary thinks plausible. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
- **Spices.** Gill links them to Sheba's frankincense trade. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/10.htm
- **Gold and gems.** Ellicott says these may have been local products or brought from further east. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-10.html
- **Devotional use.** The Biblical Illustrator applies this verse to telling Jesus all that is in our hearts. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-kings-10.html
- **A legend.** The Church Pulpit Commentary retells a story of her testing Solomon with real and fake flowers, which he solved by letting bees in. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/cpc/1-kings-10.html

**v. 3**
- Gill says Solomon solved her riddles and objections, however obscure. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-10.html

**v. 4**
- **"The palace he had built." [Debate]**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says verse 5 means the palace, not the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
  - Gill reads it as all his buildings. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/10.htm
- **Picture of Christ.** Bible Hub's notes say the queen's recognition looks ahead to Gentiles recognising Christ. https://biblehub.com/1_kings/10-4.htm

**v. 5**
- **"Seating… service."** Precept Austin says the Hebrew contrasts officials who sat with waiters who stood. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64364/
- **"Burnt offerings" or "ascent"? [Debate]**
  - Gill prefers the steps Solomon went up to the temple. He notes the Septuagint (the ancient Greek translation), the Latin Vulgate and Josephus read "burnt offerings." https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/10.htm
  - The Pulpit Commentary defends "burnt offerings." It says the huge number of sacrifices could have amazed her. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
- **"Took her breath away."** Clarke thinks she was overwhelmed or nearly fainted. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-10.html

**vv. 6–7**
- Gill says she thought the reports were exaggerated, but the reality was beyond words. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/10.htm
- The Biblical Illustrator says rumour should push us to look into the truth for ourselves, and the truth will prove greater than the rumour. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tbi/1-kings-10.html
- A devotional quoted on Precept Austin applies "not half was told" to Christ. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64364/

**v. 8**
- Enduring Word: serving Solomon was a joy, and serving Jesus is far happier. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-10/
- Henry: many have this privilege without valuing it. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-10.html
- **Catholic / Church Father.** Ambrose discusses the queen's words. He says people look for someone who combines justice with prudence, as the kings of the earth did with Solomon. https://www.newadvent.org/fathers/34012.htm

**v. 9**
- **Did she come to faith? [Debate]**
  - **No.** The Pulpit Commentary says it is unwarranted to conclude she converted. Polytheists happily honoured other nations' gods, and she says "*your* God." It also notes all her gifts went to the king, not the temple. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
  - **No.** Coffman says she probably saw the LORD as Israel's god, on a level with other gods. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-10.html
  - **No.** Guzik quotes Dilday and Wiseman calling it polite recognition. He concludes that impressive buildings and programmes are not enough to bring seekers to faith. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-kings/1-kings-10.cfm
  - **Maybe.** Gill says she may have gained better ideas of God. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/10.htm
  - **Maybe.** Waite (Pulpit Homiletics) sees mainly an honest thirst for the highest truth. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/homiletics/1_kings/10.htm
- **"Set you on the throne."**
  - Solomon was not the obvious heir, so this was God's own choice. Guzik quotes Poole on this. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-10/
  - Gill links it to Solomon's name Jedidiah, "beloved of the LORD." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/10-9.html
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia also notes Solomon was not the logical heir. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/solomon
- **"Justice and righteousness."**
  - Gill says the purpose of kingship is justice, not luxury. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-kings/10-9.html
  - Henry says rulers should care more about their duties than their honours. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-10.html
- **"Eternal love for Israel."** Butler's sermon outline reads this as a promise that Israel has a lasting future as a nation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/pdf/64364/

**v. 10**
- Gill: 120 talents is the same sum Hiram gave, and fulfils Psalm 72:15. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/gill/1_kings/10.htm
- Constable: about 4.5 tons of gold, probably part of a treaty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-10.html
- The Pulpit Commentary cites Josephus that the balsam plant came to Israel with her gifts. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
- Henry: Christ doesn't need our gifts but accepts them as thanks. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_010.cfm

**vv. 11–12**
- **Why these verses interrupt.** They are an aside. Mentioning her gold and gems reminded the writer of the fleet's cargo. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_kings/10-10.htm
- **What the almug "steps" were.** Views include steps with banisters, inlaid pavements, balusters and benches. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
- Ellicott thinks they were rails for stairs, not structural pillars. He says the wood's beauty and hardness suited harps. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-10.html

**v. 13**
- Ellicott: the wording shows she had the lower rank, and her present was a kind of tribute. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-10.html
- **The "child" legend.**
  - Coffman says this verse is the basis of a Jewish tradition that she wanted a child by Solomon. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bcc/1-kings-10.html
  - GotQuestions says such stories are speculation. https://www.gotquestions.org/Queen-of-Sheba.html
  - Bible Odyssey describes the Ethiopian Kebra Nagast tradition: a son, Menelik I, carried the Ark to Ethiopia. https://wwww.bibleodyssey.org/articles/solomon/
  - The Catholic Encyclopedia calls that Ethiopian tradition fairly recent and unconfirmed by early sources. https://www.catholic.com/encyclopedia/ethiopia
- Pulpit Homiletics quotes a writer who says the visit seems to have had no spiritual result. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm

**v. 14 (666)**
- **[Debate]** about the link with the number of the beast in Revelation 13:
  - Enduring Word connects it to the Antichrist. It suggests he may be like Solomon, a good man corrupted by power and wealth. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-10/
  - The Pulpit Commentary thinks the match is probably "not altogether accidental." It links Solomon as a "royal merchant" to the mark on buyers and sellers (Revelation 13:17). It also notes the gold could hardly have weighed exactly 666 talents every year. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
  - Precept Austin simply treats it as yearly income from trade and vassal states. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-10-commentary
- Constable: almost 25 tons a year. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-10.html

**v. 15**
- Constable: "traders" probably passed through Israel, while "merchants" did business inside it. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-10.html

**vv. 16–17**
- **Translation.** The Septuagint reads "spears." Scholars disagree whether the gold was "beaten" or "mixed," and Rawlinson thought the shields were only plated. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-10.html
- **What they were for.**
  - Enduring Word and Constable say gold is too soft for battle, so they were for show. Enduring Word adds that they gave the image of a warrior king without the substance. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-10/ and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-10.html
  - Henry reads them as a sign that Solomon used his power to protect good people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_010.cfm

**vv. 18–20**
- Ellicott: the throne was probably inlaid with ivory and gold, likely by workmen from Tyre. The lion stood for Judah, twelve matched the tribes, and the height showed majesty. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-10.html
- Gill: white ivory suggests pure justice, perhaps echoed in the "great white throne" (Revelation 20:11). The lions point to Christ, the Lion of Judah. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-10.html
- Precept Austin compares the throne to God's throne in Revelation 4. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-10-commentary
- Henry: the lions reminded Solomon to judge boldly. https://studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/1-kings-10.html
- Clarke: a round-topped chair with arms (Hebrew "hands"). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-10.html
- **Twelve or fourteen lions?** The Pulpit Commentary prefers twelve in total. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm

**v. 21**
- Precept Austin thinks this extravagance looks like flaunting wealth. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-10-commentary
- The Pulpit Commentary corrects a margin reading: "none silver" does not mean "pure, unmixed gold." https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/tpc/1-kings-10.html

**v. 22**
- **Which fleet? [Debate]**
  - The Pulpit Commentary argues for a second fleet trading with Tartessus in Spain, which ties in with the plentiful silver. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
  - Expositor's Bible places Ophir possibly at the mouth of the Indus. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/expositors/1_kings/10.htm
- Henry worries the apes and peacocks show a people grown childish through too much prosperity. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_010.cfm

**vv. 23–25**
- Precept Austin: Solomon's fame knew no limits, and sadly neither did his appetite for wealth and women. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-kings-10-commentary
- Gill: his wisdom was entirely God's gift. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/1-kings-10.html
- Clarke: the "presents" in verse 25 were tribute. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-10.html

**v. 26**
- **[Debate]**
  - The Pulpit Commentary says it broke Deuteronomy 17:16, wasn't needed in hill country, and was probably largely for show. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
  - Constable says God wanted Israel to rely on Him for protection, and Solomon fell into the trap of self-sufficiency. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/dcc/1-kings-10.html
  - Guzik suggests a strong defence may explain why there were few wars. https://www.blueletterbible.org/comm/guzik_david/study-guide/1-kings/1-kings-10.cfm
  - Ellicott says the chariots were mainly military and helped hold the kingdom together. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/1-kings-10.html

**v. 27**
- The Pulpit Commentary calls this obvious exaggeration for effect. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm
- Henry: the kingdom was as rich as the king, which pictures Christ enriching his people. https://www.blueletterbible.org/Comm/mhc/1Ki/1Ki_010.cfm

**vv. 28–29**
- These verses break Deuteronomy 17:16. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-10/ and https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/acc/1-kings-10.html
- Guzik thinks it started with rationalising, since Solomon could tell himself he was trading for other kings. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-kings-10/
- **"Kue."** The Pulpit Commentary discusses reading it as Koa or Tekoa. It says the figures were the real purchase price, not customs duty. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/1_kings/10.htm

---

**Gaps.** I found nothing usable on vv. 15, 23 and 25 beyond the brief notes above. A second search round, for the NET Bible notes, Orthodox sources and prosperity teaching, was cut off by the tool limit.
